Physiology-02.question: ১) Normal quiet breathing is accomplished almost entirely by movement of the
Physiology-02.exp:
Normal quiet breathing is accomplished almost entirely by movement of the diaphragm.

Mechanism:

  • During inspiration, the diaphragm contracts and moves downward.

  • This increases the vertical dimension of the thoracic cavity, decreasing intrathoracic pressure and allowing air to enter the lungs.

  • During expiration, the diaphragm relaxes and moves upward; expiration is mostly passive due to elastic recoil of the lungs.

Other options:

  • Internal intercostal muscle → Mainly active during forced expiration

  • External intercostal muscle → Assists inspiration but contributes less than the diaphragm

  • Rectus abdominis → Helps forced expiration by increasing abdominal pressure

Exam pearl:

  • Main muscle of quiet inspiration → Diaphragm (~75% contribution)

  • Forced expiration → Internal intercostals + abdominal muscles

  • Accessory muscles of inspiration → SCM, scalenes

Physiology-02.question: ২) Which one is called pacemaker of heart?
Physiology-02.exp:
The SA node is called the pacemaker of the heart because it has the highest rate of spontaneous depolarization and initiates each normal heartbeat.

Location:

  • Right atrium, near the opening of the superior vena cava

Function:

  • Generates electrical impulses (60–100 beats/min)

  • Controls the rhythm of the heart

  • Impulse pathway:
    SA node → AV node → Bundle of His → Purkinje fibers → Ventricular contraction

Other options:

  • AV node → Delays impulse transmission to allow ventricular filling

  • Bundle of His → Conducts impulses from AV node to ventricles

  • Purkinje fibers → Distribute impulses throughout ventricular myocardium

Exam pearl:

  • Normal pacemaker → SA node

  • AV node intrinsic rate → 40–60/min

  • Purkinje fiber rate → 20–40/min

Physiology-02.question: ৩) ERV + RV = ?
Physiology-02.exp:
ERV + RV = FRC

Where:

  • ERV (Expiratory Reserve Volume) → Maximum additional air that can be exhaled after a normal expiration

  • RV (Residual Volume) → Air remaining in lungs after maximum forced expiration

Functional Residual Capacity (FRC) is the amount of air remaining in the lungs after a normal passive expiration.

Formula:

FRC = ERV + RVFRC = ERV + RV

Other options:

  • VC (Vital Capacity) = IRV + TV + ERV

  • TLC (Total Lung Capacity) = VC + RV

  • FRV → Not a standard lung volume term

Exam pearl:

  • FRC = ERV + RV

  • VC = IRV + TV + ERV

  • TLC = IRV + TV + ERV + RV

Physiology-02.question: ৪) In Pulsus bigeminy there is abnormality in
Physiology-02.exp:
Pulsus bigeminy is a type of arrhythmia in which normal beats are regularly followed by premature beats (usually premature ventricular contractions — PVCs).

Pattern:

  • One normal heartbeat + one premature beat → repeated pattern

  • The abnormality is mainly in the rhythm of the heart, not the rate or vessel wall.

Other options:

  • Rate → Refers to heart beats per minute (e.g., tachycardia, bradycardia)

  • Volume → Refers to pulse amplitude (e.g., pulsus alternans, pulsus paradoxus)

  • Condition of vessel wall → Related to arterial diseases, not pulsus bigeminy

Exam pearl:

  • Pulsus bigeminy → Rhythm abnormality due to premature beats

  • Pulsus alternans → Alternating pulse volume

  • Pulsus paradoxus → Exaggerated fall in systolic BP during inspiration

Physiology-02.question: ৫) Helium Dilution method is used to measure all of the following except
Physiology-02.exp:
The Helium dilution method is used to measure Functional Residual Capacity (FRC) because helium is an insoluble gas that mixes with the air already present in the lungs without being absorbed.

From FRC, other lung volumes can be calculated:

  • Residual Volume (RV) = FRC − ERV

  • Total Lung Capacity (TLC) = FRC + Inspiratory Capacity (IC)

However, Vital Capacity (VC) is measured directly by spirometry, not by helium dilution.

Other options:

  • FRC → Measured by helium dilution method 

  • RV → Can be calculated from FRC 

  • TLC → Can be calculated using FRC 

  • VC → Measured by spirometry 

Exam pearl:

  • Helium dilution → FRC measurement

  • Body plethysmography → FRC (including trapped air)

  • Spirometry → TV, IRV, ERV, VC (not RV)

Physiology-02.question: ৬) At a normal heart rate the duration(second) of atrial systole is
Physiology-02.exp:
At a normal heart rate, the duration of atrial systole is approximately 0.1 second.

Cardiac cycle (at ~75 beats/min, total duration ≈ 0.8 sec):

  • Atrial systole → 0.1 sec

  • Ventricular systole → 0.3 sec

  • Complete cardiac diastole → 0.4 sec

During atrial systole:

  • Atria contract and push the remaining blood into the ventricles (atrial kick).

  • It occurs at the end of ventricular diastole.

Other options:

  • 0.3 sec → Duration of ventricular systole

  • 0.5 sec → Not a normal atrial systole duration

  • 0.7 sec → Not a cardiac cycle component duration

Exam pearl:

  • Atrial systole = 0.1 sec

  • Ventricular systole = 0.3 sec

  • Cardiac cycle = 0.8 sec at 75/min

Physiology-02.question: ৭) The normal dead space air in a young man is about ... ml
Physiology-02.exp:
The normal dead space air volume in a healthy young adult is approximately 150 ml.

Dead space refers to the volume of air in the respiratory passages that does not participate in gas exchange.

Components:

  • Anatomical dead space = air in conducting airways (nose, trachea, bronchi)

  • Normal value ≈ 2 ml/kg body weight

  • In an average adult (≈70 kg):
    2 × 70 = 140 ml ≈ 150 ml

Other options:

  • 100 ml → Lower than normal adult value

  • 200 ml & 250 ml → Higher than normal anatomical dead space

Exam pearl:

  • Normal anatomical dead space = 150 ml

  • Alveolar ventilation = (Tidal volume − Dead space) × respiratory rate

  • Tidal volume ≈ 500 ml in a normal adult

  • Effective gas exchange air per breath ≈ 500 − 150 = 350 ml

Physiology-02.question: ৮) Which initiates cardiac cycle
Physiology-02.exp:
The cardiac cycle is initiated by atrial systole (atrial contraction), which marks the beginning of a new cardiac cycle.

During atrial systole:

  • The SA node generates an impulse.

  • Atria contract and push the remaining blood into the ventricles (atrial kick).

  • It is followed by ventricular systole.

Note: In many physiology texts, the cardiac cycle is described as beginning with atrial systole, although the electrical impulse originates from the SA node before atrial contraction.

Other options:

  • Atrial diastole → Atrial relaxation phase

  • Ventricular systole → Comes after atrial systole

  • Ventricular diastole → Ventricular filling phase after contraction

Exam pearl:

  • Pacemaker of heart → SA node

  • Beginning of cardiac cycle → Atrial systole

  • Duration of one cardiac cycle → 0.8 sec (at 75 beats/min)

Physiology-02.question: ৯) The three major organs of articulation excludes
Physiology-02.exp:
The three major organs of articulation involved in speech production are:

  1. Lips

  2. Tongue

  3. Soft palate (velum)

They modify the airflow from the vocal tract to produce different speech sounds.

Hard palate is involved in articulation (especially sounds like "t", "d", "n"), but it is not considered one of the three major organs of articulation.

Other options:

  • Lips → Major articulator 

  • Tongue → Most important articulator 

  • Soft palate → Major articulator controlling oral/nasal airflow 

  • Hard palate → Not included in the major three 

Exam pearl:

  • Major organs of articulation → Lips + Tongue + Soft palate

  • Tongue = chief organ of articulation

Physiology-02.question: ১০) Ejection click occurs following which heart sound?
Physiology-02.exp:
Explanation:
Ejection click: an ejection click sound occurs immediately following the first heart sound. The sudden opening of a deformed but mobile aortic or pulmonary valve produces the ejection click.

Physiology-02.question: ১১) The blood volume of the lungs is about...ml
Physiology-02.exp:
The blood volume of the lungs is approximately 500 ml, which is about 10% of the total blood volume.

  • Total blood volume in an adult ≈ 5 liters

  • Pulmonary circulation contains about 500 ml blood

  • The lungs act as a blood reservoir and help maintain circulation.

Other options:

  • 450 ml (9%) → Close but not the standard value

  • 550 ml (11%) → Higher than normal value

  • 600 ml (12%) → Higher than normal value

Exam pearl:

  • Blood volume in lungs ≈ 500 ml (10% of total blood volume)

  • Total blood volume ≈ 5 L (7–8% of body weight)

  • Pulmonary circulation holds about 10% of total blood

Physiology-02.question: ১২) Effect of exercise on cardiac output excludes
Physiology-02.option3: Increase venous return and thus stroke volume
Physiology-02.exp:
During exercise, cardiac output increases due to:

  • Positive chronotropism → ↑ heart rate due to sympathetic stimulation

  • Positive inotropism → ↑ force of cardiac contraction

  • Increased venous return → ↑ stroke volume by Frank–Starling mechanism

However, total peripheral resistance (TPR) decreases, not increases, because:

  • Active skeletal muscles undergo vasodilation

  • More blood flow is directed to exercising muscles

Other options:

  • Positive chronotropism → Increases cardiac output ✅

  • Positive inotropism → Increases cardiac output ✅

  • ↑ Venous return → ↑ Stroke volume → Increases cardiac output ✅

  • ↑ Total peripheral resistance → Not a normal effect of exercise ❌

Exam pearl:
Exercise → ↑ Cardiac output = ↑ HR × ↑ Stroke volume

  • Sympathetic activity → ↑ HR + ↑ contractility

  • Muscle vasodilation → ↓ TPR (despite ↑ blood pressure)

Physiology-02.question: ১৩) Maximum percentage of 02 is present in
Physiology-02.exp:
The maximum percentage of oxygen (O₂) is present in atmospheric air.

Composition of air:

  • Atmospheric air: O₂ ≈ 20.93% (≈21%)

  • Humidified air: O₂ percentage decreases because water vapor dilutes other gases

  • Alveolar air: O₂ ≈ 13–14% due to exchange with blood and mixing with residual air

  • Expired air: O₂ ≈ 16% because some oxygen is absorbed by the body

Other options:

  • Humidified air → Lower O₂ concentration due to added water vapor

  • Alveolar air → Reduced O₂, increased CO₂

  • Expired air → Contains less O₂ than inspired air

Exam pearl:

  • Atmospheric air O₂ → 21%

  • Alveolar air O₂ → 13–14%

  • Expired air O₂ → ~16%

  • Alveolar CO₂ → ~5.3%

Physiology-02.question: ১৪) Which is not a part of Respiratory Unit (also called respiratory lobule)
Physiology-02.exp:
The respiratory unit (respiratory lobule) is the portion of the lung where gas exchange occurs. It begins with the respiratory bronchiole and includes:

  • Respiratory bronchioles

  • Alveolar ducts

  • Atria

  • Alveolar sacs

  • Alveoli

Terminal bronchiole is part of the conducting zone, not the respiratory unit, because it does not participate in gas exchange.

Other options:

  • Respiratory bronchiole → First part of respiratory unit 

  • Atria → Part of alveolar region and respiratory unit 

  • Alveoli → Main site of gas exchange 

Exam pearl:

  • Conducting zone → Terminal bronchiole (no gas exchange)

  • Respiratory zone → Respiratory bronchiole + alveolar ducts + alveoli (gas exchange)

Physiology-02.question: ১৫) Direct method of measurement of cardiac output
Physiology-02.exp:
The direct method of measurement of cardiac output is the Fick method.

Fick principle:

Cardiac Output=Oxygen consumptionArteriovenous oxygen differenceCardiac Output=Arteriovenous oxygen differenceOxygen consumption​

It directly calculates cardiac output based on oxygen uptake by the body and the difference in oxygen content between arterial and venous blood.

Other options:

  • Indicator method → Indirect method using indicator dilution (e.g., dye dilution)

  • Dye dilution method → A type of indicator dilution method; indirect

  • Doppler echocardiography → Non-invasive estimation of cardiac output, not a direct method

Exam pearl:

  • Direct cardiac output measurement → Fick method

  • Indicator/dye dilution → Indirect methods

  • Normal cardiac output → ~5 L/min at rest

Physiology-02.question: ১৬) What is the % of the oxygen transported from the lungs to the tissues carried in chemical combination with haemoglobin?
Physiology-02.exp:
About 97% of oxygen transported from the lungs to tissues is carried in chemical combination with haemoglobin as oxyhaemoglobin (HbO₂).

  • Oxygen binds reversibly with iron (Fe²⁺) of haemoglobin inside red blood cells.

  • Only about 3% of oxygen is transported dissolved in plasma.

Other options:

  • 3% → Oxygen dissolved in plasma 

  • 63% & 27% → Not normal physiological values

Exam pearl:

  • O₂ transport:

    • 97% → Bound to haemoglobin

    • 3% → Dissolved in plasma1 gram haemoglobin carries ≈ 1.34 ml O₂

Physiology-02.question: ১৭) Viscosity is decreased in
Physiology-02.exp:
Blood viscosity decreases in severe anaemia because the red blood cell (RBC) mass and haematocrit are reduced.

Factors affecting blood viscosity:

  • ↑ Haematocrit (RBC concentration) → ↑ viscosity

  • ↓ Haematocrit → ↓ viscosity

Other options:

  • Polycythaemia vera/hereditary polycythaemia → ↑ RBC mass → ↑ blood viscosity

  • Spherocytosis → Increased RBC abnormalities but usually not associated with decreased blood viscosity

  • Excess immunoglobulins in blood (e.g., multiple myeloma) → ↑ plasma viscosity

Exam pearl:

  • Anaemia → ↓ blood viscosity

  • Polycythaemia → ↑ blood viscosity

  • Normal blood viscosity ≈ 3–4 times that of water

Physiology-02.question: ১৮) Factors that shift 02-Hb dissociation curve to left
Physiology-02.exp:
An increase in pH shifts the oxygen–haemoglobin (O₂-Hb) dissociation curve to the left.

Left shift means:

  • Increased affinity of haemoglobin for oxygen

  • Reduced oxygen release to tissues

Factors causing left shift:

  • ↑ pH (alkalosis)

  • ↓ CO₂

  • ↓ Temperature

  • ↓ 2,3-BPG

  • Fetal haemoglobin (HbF)

Other options:

  • Increased CO₂ → Right shift (Bohr effect) → promotes oxygen unloading 

  • Increased temperature → Right shift → promotes oxygen release 

  • Increased BPG → Right shift → decreases Hb affinity for oxygen 

Exam pearl:
Left shift = “Hold O₂ tightly”
↑ pH, ↓ CO₂, ↓ temperature, ↓ BPG → ↑ Hb–O₂ affinity
Right shift = “Release O₂”
↑ CO₂, ↓ pH, ↑ temperature, ↑ BPG → ↑ tissue oxygen delivery

Physiology-02.question: ১৯) Maximum CO2 is transported as
Physiology-02.exp:
The maximum amount of carbon dioxide (CO₂) is transported in the blood as bicarbonate ions (HCO₃⁻).

CO₂ transport forms:

  • ~70% → HCO₃⁻ (bicarbonate ions) ✅

  • ~20–23% → Carbaminohaemoglobin (Hb-CO₂)

  • ~7% → Dissolved CO₂ in plasma

Mechanism:

  • In RBCs, CO₂ combines with water:

CO2+H2O→H2CO3→H++HCO3−CO2​+H2​O→H2​CO3​→H++HCO3−​

  • The enzyme carbonic anhydrase catalyzes this reaction.

Other options:

  • Dissolved state → Only small amount transported

  • Hb-CO₂ → Second major form

  • H₂CO₃ → Intermediate form, not the major transport form 

Exam pearl:
CO₂ transport: HCO₃⁻ (70%) > Carbamino-Hb (20–23%) > Dissolved CO₂ (7%)

Physiology-02.question: ২০) Pulse pressure does not depend on
Physiology-02.exp:
Pulse pressure (PP) is the difference between systolic blood pressure (SBP) and diastolic blood pressure (DBP).

Pulse Pressure = SBP - DBPPulse Pressure = SBP - DBP

It mainly depends on:

  • Stroke volume → ↑ stroke volume causes ↑ pulse pressure

  • Total peripheral resistance (TPR) → affects diastolic pressure and pulse pressure

  • Arterial elastic properties (arterial compliance) → decreased elasticity increases pulse pressure (e.g., old age)

Age itself is not a direct determining factor; rather, age-related arterial stiffness affects pulse pressure.

Other options:

  • Stroke volume → Major determinant 

  • TPR → Influences pulse pressur

  • Arterial elastic constant/compliance → Influences pulse pressure 

Exam pearl:

  • ↑ Stroke volume + ↓ arterial compliance → ↑ pulse pressure

  • Normal pulse pressure ≈ 40 mmHg

  • Wide pulse pressure → Aortic regurgitation, aging, arterial stiffness

Physiology-02.question: ২১) “When Oxygen Binds With Hemoglobin, CO2 Is Released to increase CO2 Transport”- this effect is called
Physiology-02.exp:
The Haldane effect states that when oxygen binds with haemoglobin, CO₂ is released from haemoglobin, which increases the transport of CO₂ from tissues to lungs.

Mechanism:

  • In tissues: Deoxygenated haemoglobin binds more CO₂ and H⁺ → promotes CO₂ transport.

  • In lungs: Oxygen binds to haemoglobin → decreases Hb affinity for CO₂ and H⁺ → releases CO₂ for expiration.

Other options:

  • Bohr effect → CO₂/H⁺ reduces haemoglobin affinity for O₂, causing oxygen unloading in tissues 

  • Chloride shift → Exchange of HCO₃⁻ and Cl⁻ across RBC membrane during CO₂ transport 

  • Ohm effect → Related to electrical resistance, not respiration 

Exam pearl:

  • Haldane effect = O₂ loading promotes CO₂ unloading in lungs

  • Bohr effect = CO₂/H⁺ promotes O₂ unloading in tissues

Physiology-02.question: ২২) BP on lower limb is measured over
Physiology-02.exp:
Blood pressure in the lower limb is commonly measured over the popliteal artery using a cuff placed around the thigh.

Procedure:

  • The cuff is applied to the upper thigh.

  • The stethoscope is placed over the popliteal artery in the popliteal fossa.

  • Korotkoff sounds are used to determine systolic and diastolic pressures.

Other options:

  • Anterior tibial artery → Not used for routine BP measurement 

  • Posterior tibial artery → Used for assessing peripheral pulses, not standard BP measurement 

  • Femoral artery → Major artery but not the usual auscultation site for lower limb BP 

Exam pearl:

  • Upper limb BP → Brachial artery

  • Lower limb BP → Popliteal artery

  • Lower limb systolic BP is normally higher than upper limb due to pulse amplification.

Physiology-02.question: ২৩) Which mainly controls rate and depth of breathing?
Physiology-02.exp:
he ventral respiratory centre (VRC) mainly controls the rate and depth of breathing, especially during forced breathing.

Functions:

  • Contains inspiratory and expiratory neurons

  • Becomes active when increased ventilation is required (e.g., exercise)

  • Controls the forceful contraction of respiratory muscles

Other options:

  • Dorsal respiratory centre (DRC) → Mainly controls basic rhythm of inspiration during quiet breathing 

  • Pneumotaxic centre → Limits inspiration and regulates the duration of inspiration (controls breathing pattern)

  • Apneustic centre → Promotes inspiration and prolongs inspiratory signals 

Exam pearl:

  • DRC (medulla) → basic inspiratory rhythm

  • VRC (medulla) → rate & depth of respiration (especially forced breathing)

  • Pneumotaxic centre (pons) → switches off inspiration

Physiology-02.question: ২৪) Rapidly acting BP regulating mechanisms excludes
Physiology-02.exp:
The renin–angiotensin mechanism is a slow/intermediate-term blood pressure regulatory mechanism, not a rapidly acting mechanism.

Rapidly acting BP regulatory mechanisms (seconds to minutes):

  • Baroreceptor mechanism → Detects changes in arterial pressure and rapidly adjusts sympathetic activity

  • Chemoreceptor mechanism → Responds to changes in O₂, CO₂, and H⁺ levels

  • CNS ischemic mechanism → Powerful emergency mechanism activated during severe hypotension

Renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system (RAAS):

  • Takes minutes to hours to act

  • Increases BP by vasoconstriction (angiotensin II) and sodium/water retention (aldosterone)

Exam pearl:
Fast BP control → Baroreceptor + Chemoreceptor + CNS ischemic response
Slow BP control → RAAS + renal fluid mechanism

Physiology-02.question: ২৫) The ultimate goal of respiration is to maintain proper concentrations of the following in the tissues except?
Physiology-02.exp:
The ultimate goal of respiration is to maintain proper concentrations of O₂, CO₂, and H⁺ in the tissues, thereby maintaining acid–base balance and normal cellular metabolism.

  • O₂ → Required for aerobic metabolism and ATP production

  • CO₂ → Must be removed to prevent accumulation and acidosis 

  • H⁺ → Regulated to maintain normal pH of body fluids 

  • HCO₃⁻ → Mainly acts as a buffer system in blood and helps transport CO₂, but it is not considered a direct tissue gas concentration controlled by respiration 

Exam pearl:
Respiration primarily regulates:

  • O₂ concentration

  • CO₂ concentration

  • H⁺ concentration (pH)

Major respiratory function → Maintain O₂ supply and remove CO₂ to keep acid–base balance.

Physiology-02.question: ২৬) Which are called stopclocks of circulation?
Physiology-02.exp:
Explanation:
Arterioles are the major site of the resistance to blood flow. So, arterioles are the stopclocks' of the circulation.

Physiology-02.question: ৩০) Definite cyanosis appears whenever the arterial blood contains more than …. grams of deoxygenated hemoglobin in each 100 ml of blood?
Physiology-02.exp:
Definite cyanosis appears when the arterial blood contains more than 5 g of deoxygenated haemoglobin per 100 ml of blood.

Cyanosis occurs due to increased reduced (deoxygenated) haemoglobin in the blood, causing bluish discoloration of skin and mucous membranes.

Important points:

  • Threshold for visible cyanosis → ≥ 5 g/dL reduced Hb

  • In severe anaemia, cyanosis may be difficult to detect because total haemoglobin is low.

  • In polycythaemia, cyanosis may appear more easily due to increased total Hb.

Other options:

  • 3 g → Below the usual threshold 

  • 4 g → Below the usual threshold 

  • 7 g → Higher than required 

Exam pearl:
Cyanosis appears when reduced Hb > 5 g/100 ml blood.

Physiology-02.question: ৩২) Primary expiratory muscle
Physiology-02.exp:
The primary expiratory muscles are the internal intercostal muscles, especially during forced expiration.

Mechanism:

  • Internal intercostal muscles contract → pull ribs downward and inward → decrease thoracic volume → force air out of the lungs.

Other options:

  • Diaphragm → Primary muscle of quiet inspiration; relaxation assists normal expiration 

  • Sternocleidomastoid → Accessory muscle of inspiration (especially during respiratory distress) 

  • External intercostal muscles → Assist inspiration by elevating ribs 

Exam pearl:

  • Quiet inspiration → Diaphragm + external intercostals

  • Forced expiration → Internal intercostals + abdominal muscles

  • Accessory inspiratory muscle → Sternocleidomastoid

Physiology-02.question: ৩৫) Maximum % of total blood that can be removed with almost no effect on cardiac output?
Physiology-02.exp:
About 20% of total blood volume can be removed with almost no immediate effect on cardiac output because the body can compensate through:

  • Venoconstriction → mobilizes blood from venous reservoirs

  • Increased heart rate

  • Increased sympathetic activity → maintains blood pressure and cardiac output

Normal adult blood volume ≈ 5 liters.
20% removal ≈ 1 liter, which can initially be compensated.

Physiology-02.question: ৩৬) Stages of shock excludes
Physiology-02.exp:
The classical stages of shock are:

  1. Non-progressive (compensated) stage → Body compensatory mechanisms maintain tissue perfusion.

  2. Progressive stage → Inadequate perfusion leads to worsening circulatory failure.

  3. Irreversible stage → Severe cellular injury and organ failure occur despite treatment.

Transitional stage is not a recognized classical stage of shock.

Exam pearl:
Stages of shock = Non-progressive → Progressive → Irreversible.

Physiology-02.question: ৩৭) Manifestations of shock includes all of the following except?
Physiology-02.exp:
Shock is a state of inadequate tissue perfusion, causing compensatory responses to maintain oxygen delivery.

Common manifestations include:

  • ↓ Cardiac output → due to reduced circulating volume or cardiac dysfunction

  • Low blood pressure (hypotension) → especially in severe shock

  • Rapid, thready pulse → due to sympathetic activation and reduced stroke volume

Respiratory response in shock is usually:

  • ↑ Respiratory rate (tachypnoea) to compensate for tissue hypoxia and metabolic acidosis.

Exam pearl:
Shock features:

  • ↓ Cardiac output

  • ↓ Blood pressure

  • ↑ Heart rate (rapid thready pulse)

  • ↑ Respiratory rate (not decreased)

Physiology-02.question: ৪১) The normal pleural pressure at the beginning of inspiration is about .... centimeters of water (cm H2O)?
Physiology-02.exp:
The normal pleural pressure at the beginning of inspiration is about -5 cm H₂O.

During quiet breathing:

  • At the end of expiration → pleural pressure ≈ -5 cm H₂O

  • During inspiration → thoracic expansion makes pleural pressure more negative (around -7.5 cm H₂O)

The negative intrapleural pressure helps keep the lungs expanded by maintaining a transpulmonary pressure gradient.

Exam pearl:

  • Normal pleural pressure at rest = −5 cm H₂O

  • During inspiration = becomes more negative (≈ −7.5 cm H₂O)

  • During forced expiration = may become positive.

Physiology-02.question: ৪২) Ventricular repolarisation in ECG is represented by
Physiology-02.exp:
Explanation:
Ventricular repolarisation in ECG is represented by the T wave.

ECG waves:

  • P wave → Atrial depolarisation

  • QRS complex → Ventricular depolarisation

  • T wave → Ventricular repolarisation 

  • ST segment → Period when ventricles are fully depolarised (plateau phase), not repolarisation itself

Exam pearl:
P = Atrial depolarisation
QRS = Ventricular depolarisation
T = Ventricular repolarisation

Physiology-02.question: ৪৩) Difference between Alveolar and Pleural Pressures is called
Physiology-02.exp:
The difference between alveolar pressure and pleural pressure is called transpulmonary

Exam pearl:

  • Transpulmonary pressure = Pᴀʟᴠ − Pᴘʟ → keeps lungs open

  • Normal value at rest ≈ +5 cm H₂O

pressure.

Physiology-02.question: ৪৪) Bifid broad P wave indicates hypertrophy of
Physiology-02.exp:
A bifid broad P wave on ECG indicates left atrial hypertrophy (LAH).

  • It is called “P mitrale” because it is classically seen in mitral stenosis.

  • The P wave becomes:

    • Wide (>0.12 sec)

    • Notched/bifid (“M-shaped”) in leads I and II

  • It occurs due to delayed conduction through the enlarged left atrium.

Exam pearl:

  • Left atrial hypertrophy → Broad, bifid P wave (P mitrale)

  • Right atrial hypertrophy → Tall, peaked P wave (P pulmonale)

  • Ventricular hypertrophy → Mainly affects QRS complex, not P wave

Physiology-02.question: ৪৫) The most important components of surfactant
Physiology-02.exp:
The most important component of pulmonary surfactant is Dipalmitoyl phosphatidylcholine (DPPC), also called lecithin.

Functions of surfactant:

  • Reduces surface tension at the alveolar air–fluid interface

  • Prevents alveolar collapse (atelectasis), especially during expiration

  • Increases lung compliance

Surfactant is produced by Type II alveolar pneumocytes.

Exam pearl:

  • Major surfactant phospholipid → DPPC (lecithin)

  • Source → Type II pneumocytes

  • Deficiency → Neonatal respiratory distress syndrome (RDS) due to increased alveolar surface tension.

Physiology-02.question: ৪৬) Which is indicator of ventricular rate?
Physiology-02.exp:
The RR interval is an indicator of the ventricular rate in ECG.

  • The RR interval is the time between two consecutive R waves (two ventricular depolarizations).

  • Ventricular heart rate can be calculated from RR interval:

Heart rate=60RR interval (seconds)Heart rate=RR interval (seconds)60​

Other ECG components:

  • PR interval → Represents conduction time from atria to ventricles (AV conduction) 

  • QRS complex → Represents ventricular depolarisation, not rate measurement 

  • ST segment → Represents ventricular plateau phase after depolarisation 

Exam pearl:

  • Ventricular rate → RR interval

  • Atrial rate → PP interval

  • Ventricular depolarisation → QRS complex

  • Ventricular repolarisation → T wave

Physiology-02.question: ৪৭) The extra volume of air that can be inspired over and above the normal tidal volume when the person inspires with full force is called
Physiology-02.exp:
The extra volume of air that can be inspired forcefully after a normal tidal inspiration is called Inspiratory Reserve Volume (IRV).

Lung volumes:

  • Tidal volume (TV) → Air inspired or expired during normal quiet breathing (~500 mL)

  • Inspiratory reserve volume (IRV) → Additional air that can be inspired with maximum effort after normal inspiration (~3000 mL) 

  • Expiratory reserve volume (ERV) → Additional air that can be expired forcefully after normal expiration (~1100 mL) 

  • Residual volume (RV) → Air remaining in lungs after maximum expiration (~1200 mL) 

Exam pearl:
IRV = Extra air inspired after normal inspiration
ERV = Extra air expired after normal expiration
RV = Air left after maximum expiration
TV = Normal breath (~500 mL)

Physiology-02.question: ৪৮) Heart rate may increase in
Physiology-02.exp:
Heart rate increases when the sympathetic nervous system is stimulated.

Sympathetic stimulation releases noradrenaline (norepinephrine) at the SA node, causing:

  • ↑ SA node firing rate

  • ↑ Heart rate (positive chronotropic effect)

Other conditions:

  • Fear → Activates sympathetic system → ↑ heart rate (also increases HR)

  • Sleep → Increased parasympathetic activity → ↓ heart rate

  • Hypothyroidism → Reduced metabolic activity → Usually causes bradycardia

Exam pearl:

  • Sympathetic stimulation → ↑ Heart rate

  • Parasympathetic (vagus) stimulation → ↓ Heart rate

  • Thyrotoxicosis → Tachycardia

  • Hypothyroidism → Bradycardia

Physiology-02.question: ৪৯) Total lung capacity (ml) in women
Physiology-02.exp:
The normal Total Lung Capacity (TLC) in women is approximately 4200–4600 ml. The standard value commonly used in physiology MCQs is ≈4600 ml.

Total Lung Capacity (TLC):

TLC=Vital Capacity (VC)+Residual Volume (RV)TLC=Vital Capacity (VC)+Residual Volume (RV)

Approximate values:

  • Male TLC → ~5800–6000 ml

  • Female TLC → ~4200–4600 ml

Exam pearl:

  • TLC (male) ≈ 5800 ml

  • TLC (female) ≈ 4600 ml

  • Female lung volumes are generally lower due to smaller body size and lung dimensions.

Physiology-02.question: ৫০) Pathological causes of sinus bradycardia excludes
Physiology-02.exp:
Fever is not a cause of sinus bradycardia; instead, fever usually causes sinus tachycardia.

Rule:

  • For every 1°C rise in body temperature, heart rate usually increases by about 10–15 beats/min due to increased metabolic demand.

Causes of sinus bradycardia include:

  • Hypothyroidism → reduced metabolic activity → ↓ heart rate

  • Myocardial infarction (especially inferior wall MI) → increased vagal tone affecting SA node → bradycardia 

  • Raised intracranial pressure → increased vagal stimulation (Cushing reflex component) → bradycardia 

Exam pearl:
Fever → Tachycardia
Hypothermia, hypothyroidism, inferior MI, raised ICP → Bradycardia
